intro: EVA is a series of operations: building the body in the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory's giant pool, preventing decompression sickness through pre-breathe, and exiting from Quest into the vacuum. Spacewalking is not swimming.
lessons.0.title: Neutral buoyancy is a substitute for microgravity, not microgravity itself
lessons.0.summary: Water retains inertia and viscosity. Nevertheless, it allows the longest on-Earth repetition of the sensation of handling a full-size spacesuit in three dimensions.
lessons.0.body.0: The official candidate course places EVA skills training and scuba certification as pillars of the basic curriculum. The Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory at Johnson's Sonny Carter Training Facility is a giant tank with a full-scale ISS mockup submerged in it. Candidates repeat tasks here while wearing spacesuits.
lessons.0.body.1: Underwater, if you match neutral buoyancy, you 'do not sink.' However, water resists every hand movement and damps rotation. In orbital vacuum, a body set in motion continues to rotate. What is learned in the NBL is the habit of using handrails and footholds, and determining the body's axis first.
lessons.0.body.2: Official summer reports record that the 2025 class began EVA training in the NBL. The same tank is also used for water survival raft and storm training. Do not fear water, but do not over-trust it.
lessons.0.facts.0.label: Facility
lessons.0.facts.1.label: Purpose
lessons.0.deepDive.title: What neutral buoyancy cancels and what remains
lessons.0.deepDive.body.0: Even if the net force of weight and buoyancy is minimized, the inertia of the body and suit remains. Furthermore, because water resistance damps motion, movements that stop easily underwater do not necessarily stop the same way in orbit. When learning to use handrails and footholds, be aware of this difference.
lessons.0.deepDive.body.1: Where weights and floats are attached affects not only the net force but also rotation. This game displays fore-aft and left-right moments separately. If you tilt without sinking or floating, it is an exercise in reviewing the placement, not just the total mass.
lessons.1.title: The pool is made of time, safety divers, and mockups
lessons.1.summary: What is visible is not just blue water. It is time limits, abort criteria, and full-scale walls.
lessons.1.body.0: NBL training runs are limited by dive time, suit heat, and diver fatigue. Even if an orbital EVA lasts a few hours, underwater preparation and cleanup take longer than the main task. The official course requires scuba first to embody underwater self-preservation before the suit.
lessons.1.body.1: Mockups reproduce the exterior walls of Quest, trusses, and lab modules. Tool placement, foot restraints, and cable routing are arranged with the same numbers as the actual procedure manuals. The 'left handrail' learned here is the left handrail on the night side of orbit as well.
lessons.1.body.2: Water clarity, lighting, and bubbles can make visibility better or worse than in a real EVA. Water leaking inside the helmet is a suffocation risk repeatedly warned about in official EVA anomaly explanations. In the NBL as well, water in front of the face must be reported immediately.
lessons.1.facts.0.label: Prerequisite
lessons.1.facts.1.label: Contents
lessons.2.title: The EMU is a spacecraft cut out for just one person
lessons.2.summary: Life support, pressurization, communications, cooling, and power are contained within the hard upper torso and gloves.
lessons.2.body.0: The U.S. Extravehicular Mobility Unit (EMU) is the primary equipment for exiting the ISS's Quest. Official Quest explanations state that entry and exit via U.S. spacesuits is the main path through this airlock, noting that the Orlan suit can also provide support. The interior of the suit is a low-pressure pure oxygen environment, differing in both composition and pressure from the nearly 1-atmosphere air inside the spacecraft.
lessons.2.body.1: This difference is the cause of decompression sickness (DCS). Nitrogen in the body can form bubbles. Pre-breathe is the time required to wash out nitrogen before lowering the pressure. OCHMO's explanation of decompression sickness serves as the basis for the procedure selection minigame in this lesson.
lessons.2.body.2: Gloves are the bottleneck of work. Official EVA anomaly collections list fatigue, burns, cold, CO2, eye irritation, ammonia, and water inside the helmet. Behind the beautiful images of weightlessness lies this list.
lessons.2.facts.0.label: Main path
lessons.2.facts.1.label: Atmosphere
lessons.3.title: Weight-out is the work of finding the point that neither floats nor sinks
lessons.3.summary: Match weights and floats in fore-aft, left-right, and net buoyancy. If not neutral, work becomes a struggle against posture.
lessons.3.body.0: In the NBL, the placement of weights and floats is changed for each combination of suit and person. If the net is positive, it rises to the ceiling; if negative, it sinks to the floor. If it is heavy in front, it pitches down; if biased left or right, it rolls. The minigame has three gauges because the on-site adjustment involves three degrees of freedom.
lessons.3.body.1: There are no weights in orbit. Instead, the same 'fixed axis' is created using foot restraints, handrails, and the body's inertia. Weight-out training teaches the intuition that mass distribution determines work precision.
lessons.3.body.2: Alignment is not a one-time event. Holding tools changes buoyancy, as does the remaining tank level. The scene of a diver making fine adjustments mid-run is a rehearsal for the 'accumulation of small forces' in the actual mission.
lessons.3.facts.0.label: Axis
lessons.3.facts.1.label: Orbital Equivalent
lessons.4.title: Mockups are the 3D version of the procedure manual
lessons.4.summary: If a bolt is off by a few centimeters, hours in orbit are lost. The pool walls are built to not allow for such deviations.
lessons.4.body.0: NBL mockups reproduce the ISS truss and module exterior walls at a distance where divers can touch them. Tool bag placement, tether routing, and foot restraint holes carry the same numbers as flight procedures. Steps that are 'assumed' here will return to haunt you on the night side of the actual mission.
lessons.4.body.1: Official EVA anomaly explanations categorize issues into hardware damage, mission failure, and injury. Mockup training is a low-cost way to fail, simulating tool drops (which sink in water but fly away in orbit) and musculoskeletal pain from forced postures.
lessons.4.body.2: Camera placement is also part of the mockup. The video seen on the ground and by the crew is not their own eyes. The lesson shared with robotics is to move hands to the surface captured by the camera without moving the head.
lessons.4.facts.0.label: Fidelity
lessons.4.facts.1.label: Fail Cheaply
lessons.5.title: Safety divers are the invisible ground crew
lessons.5.summary: The person in the suit cannot fully see their own back or feet. Others in the water become the eyes for abort criteria.
lessons.5.body.0: NBL runs include safety and utility divers. Official photos show divers conversing with raft candidates even during water landing training. In EVA training, they handle weight fine-tuning, untangling, and decisions on emergency ascents.
lessons.5.body.1: There are no divers in orbit. Instead, crew-to-crew tether checks, ground video, and suit telemetry fulfill the same role. The habit learned at NBL of 'verbalizing unseen parts' by borrowing a diver's perspective becomes the lifeline of two-person EVAs.
lessons.5.body.2: Aborting is not failure. Water in the helmet, rising CO2, glove pain, ammonia smell. These signs listed in official anomaly collections must be immediately relayed to the ground team acting as the diver.
lessons.5.facts.0.label: Underwater
lessons.5.facts.1.label: In Orbit
lessons.6.title: Quest is the room for dressing and the room for exiting to vacuum
lessons.6.summary: Maintenance in the equipment lock, depressurization in the crew lock. Mishandling the hatch endangers the cabin.
lessons.6.body.0: Quest is a pressurized module with an equipment lock and crew lock connected in series by a bulkhead and hatch. Official Quick Facts state a length of 18 feet, a diameter of 13.1 feet, and a mass of 21,877 pounds. It is the primary path for the US EMU, having been attached in July 2001 on STS-104.
lessons.6.body.1: Some prebreathes, such as Campout, involve spending the night in the airlock lowered to around 10.2 psi. This system is addressed by OCHMO decompression sickness explanations and this Academy's procedure selection. The equipment lock is not a 'changing room' but a device room for life support and depressurization.
lessons.6.body.2: Hatch opening/closing order, equalization, and leak checks are the mirror image of emergency depressurization procedures. The procedures become symmetrically strict when exiting and when returning to bake out ammonia.
lessons.6.facts.0.label: Compartments
lessons.6.facts.1.label: Attachment
lessons.7.title: Prebreathe is a prescription of time, pressure, and exercise
lessons.7.summary: There is not just one way to prevent decompression sickness. The situation dictates the choice of In-Suit, Campout, Exercise, or ISLE.
lessons.7.body.0: The OCHMO Technical Brief (Decompression Sickness) is the primary source for procedure selection in this module. The cabin is approximately 14.7 psi of air, while the EMU is low-pressure pure oxygen. Reducing pressure without reducing nitrogen can cause bubbles in tissues.
lessons.7.body.1: In-Suit involves breathing pure oxygen for about 4 hours inside the suit at 14.7 psi. It is simple but long. Campout involves spending the night in the airlock at 10.2 psi and 26.5% oxygen, shortening the in-suit time on the day of the mission. The exercise method combines short, high-intensity exercise under pure oxygen, while ISLE involves 40 minutes of mask breathing, 20 minutes of decompression, and repeated light exercise in the suit.
lessons.7.body.2: The final question in the mini-game is that gravity remains on the lunar surface, meaning ISS microgravity protocols cannot be directly transplanted. Gravity alters the distribution and circulation of nitrogen. Planetary EVA requires a different prescription.
lessons.7.facts.0.label: Basis
lessons.7.facts.1.label: Variables
lessons.8.title: In an EVA timeline, life support precedes science
lessons.8.summary: Oxygen, cooling, CO2, tethers, and sunlight run out before the next step in tool usage.
lessons.8.body.0: Official EVA anomaly explanations position planned shortfalls as occurring in the same frequency band as hardware failures and injuries. The causes are the accumulation of issues related to visibility, heat, CO2, tools, and fatigue. The timeline is a frame cut by life support reserves, not a greedy work list.
lessons.8.body.1: Sunlight and shadow alter heat, power generation, and camera exposure. The ISS's 90-minute orbit crosses multiple day-night cycles during a long EVA. Before the next night side, one must decide whether to finish the current connector or return.
lessons.8.body.2: Ground control monitors suit telemetry. Crew members report their sensations in a single word. Omission is the same habit that breaks the room in later emergency drills.
lessons.8.facts.0.label: Frame
lessons.8.facts.1.label: Shortfall
lessons.9.title: Planetary EVA is not an extension of the pool
lessons.9.summary: The lunar surface has 1/6 G gravity, dust, and permanent shadows. NBL neutral buoyancy does not replicate all of these.
lessons.9.body.0: NBL is optimized for ISS exterior work. Feet enter hooks, and the body floats in three dimensions. On the lunar surface, feet are on the ground, and falling, dust, and long shadows become the main enemies. This is why official geological field training develops observation, navigation, and teamwork through separate pathways.
lessons.9.body.1: Decompression sickness protocols must also be reinterpreted based on the presence or absence of gravity. The pre-breathe mini-game errs by assuming 'direct validity,' which reflects a failure to translate OCHMO's concerns into learning.
lessons.9.body.2: The badge for this module is a mark of having approached neutral buoyancy in the pool and selected a pre-breathe appropriate to the situation. The qualification to collect lunar rocks must wait for the geology module.
lessons.9.facts.0.label: NBL Strength
lessons.9.facts.1.label: NBL Weakness
quiz.0.prompt: Which is the appropriate reason why NBL is not a complete reproduction of weightlessness?
quiz.0.choices.0: Because water retains viscosity and inertia
quiz.0.explanation: Neutral buoyancy provides the sensation of not falling, but water dampens movement. In a vacuum, rotation does not stop.
quiz.1.prompt: Which module is officially listed as a primary path for extravehicular activity with the US EMU?
quiz.1.explanation: Quest is the primary path for entering and exiting the US spacesuit, and it is officially noted that Orlan can also provide support.
quiz.2.prompt: Which are the two correct sections of Quest?
quiz.2.explanation: The Equipment Lock is for suit maintenance, and the Crew Lock is the actual exit.
quiz.3.prompt: What is the fundamental reason pre-breathe is necessary?
quiz.3.choices.3: To reduce nitrogen before moving to low-pressure pure oxygen
quiz.3.explanation: If depressurization occurs without washing out the nitrogen in cabin air, the risk of decompression sickness (DCS) increases.
quiz.4.prompt: What is the method of spending the previous night in the airlock at 10.2 psi and shortening the in-suit time on the day of the EVA?
quiz.4.explanation: Campout involves spending the previous night at 10.2 psi with 26.5% oxygen, shortening the pre-breathe on the day of the EVA.
quiz.5.prompt: What are the three axes aligned simultaneously in weight-out?
quiz.5.explanation: The placement of weights and floats simultaneously determines sinking/floating, forward/backward tilt, and left/right tilt.
quiz.6.prompt: What is the reason official EVA anomaly explanations view liquid inside the helmet as dangerous?
quiz.6.choices.2: There is a risk of asphyxiation or drowning
quiz.6.explanation: OCHMO's EVA mishaps state that sufficient liquid inside the helmet poses a risk of asphyxiation or drowning.
quiz.7.prompt: Which shuttle flight was responsible for the Quest integration?
quiz.7.explanation: Quest was integrated in July 2001, during Assembly 7A, on STS-104.
quiz.8.prompt: What water-related preparation does the 2011 official explanation require before the flight curriculum?
quiz.8.choices.0: Military water survival and scuba diving prepared for EVA
quiz.8.explanation: Candidates complete water survival before the flight syllabus and obtain scuba certification in preparation for extravehicular activity.
quiz.9.prompt: Which is a correct characteristic of the In-Suit protocol?
quiz.9.choices.1: Breathing pure oxygen inside the suit for an extended time at 14.7 psi
quiz.9.explanation: In-Suit is simple but takes the most time. It involves flushing nitrogen out while maintaining cabin pressure inside the suit.
quiz.10.prompt: What is the main reason ISS prebreathe protocols cannot be directly transferred to the lunar surface?
quiz.10.choices.0: Because the Moon has an atmosphere
quiz.10.choices.1: Because time is infinite on the lunar surface
quiz.10.choices.2: Because the presence or absence of gravity can alter nitrogen distribution and circulation
quiz.10.choices.3: Because pure oxygen is prohibited on the lunar surface
quiz.10.explanation: Gravity on a planetary surface can influence circulation and nitrogen handling. The mini-game also treats 'directly applicable' as incorrect.
quiz.11.prompt: What is the primary framework this lesson uses to define the EVA timeline?
quiz.11.choices.2: Only a greedy list of experiments
quiz.11.choices.3: Life support factors such as oxygen, cooling, CO2, and sunlight
quiz.11.explanation: Before the work list, suit reserves, heat, and day/night cycles determine the framework. Falling short is one category of anomaly.
quiz.12.prompt: Which is correct regarding the atmosphere inside the EMU?
quiz.12.explanation: The difference in pressure and composition between cabin air and the suit necessitates prebreathe.
quiz.13.prompt: What role in orbit corresponds to a safety diver in NBL?
quiz.13.choices.1: Visual checks by a partner, ground video, and suit telemetry
quiz.13.explanation: Others and ground data compensate for the unseen back and feet. The habit of reporting is established first in NBL.
quiz.14.prompt: Which of the following is included in the three main categories of EVA anomalies defined by official standards?
quiz.14.choices.2: Hardware damage, mission shortfall, and injury
quiz.14.explanation: OCHMO-TB-040 organizes these as hardware, crew/mission, and mission shortfall (and combinations thereof).
quiz.15.prompt: What sequence does this lesson use to introduce ISLE (In-Suit Light Exercise)?
quiz.15.choices.3: 40 minutes of pure oxygen via mask, 20 minutes to 10.2 psi, and light exercise inside the suit
quiz.15.explanation: ISLE is taught as a method involving 40 minutes on a mask, 20 minutes of depressurization, and light exercise inside the suit.
glossary.0.description: Work performed outside a pressurized vehicle. On the ISS, this is primarily done via Quest and EMU, with training repeated at NBL.
glossary.1.description: The large pool at the Sonny Carter Training Facility. ISS mockups are submerged here to train for spacesuit work.
glossary.2.description: The U.S. spacesuit. It contains a life support system for one person using low-pressure pure oxygen.
glossary.3.description: A condition where nitrogen bubbles form in tissues due to pressure reduction. It is prevented by prebreathe.
glossary.4.description: A procedure combining pure oxygen breathing, staged depressurization, and sometimes exercise to flush out nitrogen.
glossary.5.description: A method of spending the night in the airlock at around 10.2 psi to shorten the in-suit prebreathe on the day of the EVA.
glossary.6.description: The process at NBL of placing weights and floats to adjust net buoyancy and posture to neutral.
glossary.7.description: The main airlock of the ISS, consisting of a hardware lock and a crew lock.
glossary.8.description: A safety line connecting the crew and tools to the vehicle. Objects that detach do not return in orbit.
